name: Telescoping Effect
description: People can misremember when an event happened, pulling distant events forward or pushing recent events backward relative to their true date. The event is remembered, but its position in time is reconstructed inaccurately.
design_relevance_note: Most relevant to recall-based surveys, retrospective UX research, activity histories, journaling, and any product that asks users to date past behavior from memory. It has thin direct relevance to mainstream interface pattern work outside those research or logging contexts.
myth_risk_note: Keyes, Martins, Blanco & Hasin (2010) found little evidence for a telescoping effect specifically in women across two national alcohol-dependence surveys, suggesting the effect is moderated by demographic factors rather than universal. Johnson & Schultz (2005) and Carey, Garrett, Jackman, Sanders & Kalsbeek (1995) document genuine forward telescoping in other domains (smoking onset, low-back-pain episode recall), but effect size and generalizability clearly vary by population and context.
prevalence_note: A standard term in survey and autobiographical-memory research, but seldom named in ordinary product-design practice except by research-methods-aware teams.

findings.description: A very large (N=82,122) repeated cross-sectional survey study found clear evidence of forward telescoping in self-reported smoking-onset age: as age at interview increased from 12 to 25, the probability of reporting an early onset dropped by half, and the bias differed significantly by sex and race, causing real misclassification of smokers by onset timing and biasing cohort comparisons drawn from cross-sectional data. A large, independent, real-world demonstration of forward telescoping distinct from the corpus's existing diary-study evidence, using a completely different method (large-scale survey epidemiology, not diary tracking) and domain (smoking-onset self-report, not general event dating).
findings.source_title: Forward telescoping bias in reported age of onset: an example from cigarette smoking
findings.source_venue: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research

findings.description: When people date naturally occurring remembered events, they systematically misplace those events in time in ways consistent with telescoping, pulling some events toward the present and misdating others backward relative to their actual occurrence.
findings.source_title: Telescoping in dating naturally occurring events
